[Physiotherapy in intensive care units in Germany, Austria, and Switzerland: tasks, developments, and challenges].
articles.abstract: Physiotherapy in intensive care units across the German-speaking region of Europe (Germany, Austria, and Switzerland-DACH) plays a central role in interprofessional early rehabilitation. Based on multimodal approaches and evidence-based assessments, it improves functional quality of life and reduces the incidence of post-intensive care syndrome. National and international guidelines establish early rehabilitation-ideally commencing within 72 h-as the standard of care. However, there is significant heterogeneity in physiotherapy training across these three countries. This article aims to outline the differences and similarities regarding education and the implementation of physiotherapeutic interventions in the intensive care setting.

articles.title: [Medical care of nontraumatic patients in the resuscitation room].
articles.abstract: Standardized resuscitation room algorithms exist for major trauma, but systematic pathways for nontraumatic emergencies have historically been lacking. Systematic presentation of epidemiological data and consensus-based quality criteria for nontraumatic resuscitation room management. Evaluation of recent epidemiological studies (OBSERvE, OBSERvE-DUS, monocentric and multicentric cohorts) and analysis of the recommendations of the DGINA white paper. Nontraumatic emergencies constitute up to 66.6% of all resuscitation room treatments. This older, comorbid population shows a 30-day mortality of up to 36.3%. The DGINA white paper provides a consensus-based framework for structural, technical, and staff qualifications. Due to high diagnostic heterogeneity and frequent secondary specialty shifts (17.0% to 29.5%), interdisciplinary emergency medicine expertise is essential. Resuscitation room care requires overcoming monodisciplinary approaches. Clinical emergency medicine acts as a coordinating specialty to optimize diagnostic pathways and interface management. Establishing a national registry is necessary for quality assurance.

articles.title: Micromobility crashes: A review of the demographics, risk factors, injury patterns, and preventative strategies.
articles.abstract: Micromobility device use has rapidly expanded since the last several decades, largely driven by their flexibility and utility for short-distance travel. This growth has been accompanied by a corresponding rise in the rate of micromobility-related injuries and fatalities, yet the demographic patterns, risk factors, and injury characteristics associated with these incidents remain incompletely characterized. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on micromobility user demographics, injury patterns, and modifiable risk factors and evaluates proposed strategies for improving rider and pedestrian safety. Injured riders are predominantly young and male, with alcohol use, helmet non-use, excessive speed, and nighttime riding as the most consistently identified risk factors. These behaviors frequently co-occur and may have compounding effects on injury severity. Falls represent the most common injury mechanism, though collisions with motor vehicles are associated with disproportionately severe outcomes, including traumatic brain injury. Injury rates and patterns vary meaningfully by device type, though comparisons across studies are complicated by inconsistent exposure measurements and the lack of a universally standardized definition of micromobility devices. Existing legislation on impaired riding, helmet use, and sidewalk riding varies widely across jurisdictions. Emerging evidence from cities that have implemented targeted regulatory interventions, including speed and nighttime restrictions, suggests that policy measures can meaningfully reduce injury incidence. Reducing the burden of micromobility-related injuries will require a coordinated, multifaceted approach integrating improved injury surveillance, appropriate infrastructure, rider and public education, and evidence-based policy implementation.

articles.title: Motorcycle gas-tank associated pelvic trauma: A scoping review of reported injury patterns, management and outcomes.
articles.abstract: Motorcycle gas-tank contact has been implicated in pelvic ring injury, often as part of a broader polytrauma presentation. This scoping review mapped reported injury morphology, associated injuries, management and outcomes according to the strength of tank-contact evidence. This scoping review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA-ScR guidance. MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Scopus and Web of Science databases were searched from inception to 20 September 2026. English-language clinical and forensic reports linking gas-tank contact to individually extractable pelvic ring injuries were included. Aggregate studies provided separate contextual evidence. Four contact-evidence tiers were grouped into higher-certainty and lower-certainty or inferred contact. Findings were synthesised descriptively using assessable denominators. Twenty studies reported 27 patients: 10 with higher-certainty and 17 with lower-certainty evidence of gas tank contact. Posterior-ring involvement was documented in 92% (22/24) of assessable patients while combined anterior-posterior injury occurred in 75% (18/24) assessable patients. Urinary, genital or perineal/scrotal/groin injury was documented in all patients in each group. Definitive pelvic fixation was reported in 15 patients with status unreported in 9 patients. Three deaths were reported. Follow-up was reported in 52% (14/27) of patients; mean follow-up was 8.3 months. Published gas tank-associated cases show recurring combined anterior-posterior pelvic ring disruption with adjacent genital or perineal trauma. Although selective reporting and uncertain contact attribution prevent confirmation of a gas tank-specific mechanism, these findings highlight the extent of pelvic ring involvement and associated soft-tissue injury. These findings provide an anatomical basis for future studies linking injury morphology with independently documented road traffic collision mechanisms.

articles.title: Metabolic-inflammatory phenotypes and distinct mortality profiles in middle-aged and older U.S. adults: a latent profile analysis of NHANES 1999-2010.
articles.abstract: Metabolic and inflammatory abnormalities are closely involved in the development of cardiometabolic disease, yet their integrated patterns and prognostic significance remain incompletely understood. This study aimed to identify distinct metabolic-inflammatory phenotypes and evaluate their associations with all-cause and cardiovascular mortality in U.S. adults. A total of 6,236 participants aged ≥ 40 years from NHANES 1999-2010 were included. Latent profile analysis (LPA) was performed using six metabolic-inflammatory indicators, including white blood cell count (WBC), C-reactive protein (CRP), triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index, triglyceride-to-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (TG/HDL-C) ratio, body mass index (BMI), and waist circumference (WC). Survey-weighted Cox regression, Kaplan-Meier analysis, subgroup analysis, and Fine-Gray competing-risk regression were performed to evaluate associations between metabolic-inflammatory phenotypes and mortality outcomes. Four distinct phenotypes were identified: Healthy, Mild obesity-inflammatory, Severe dysmetabolic, and Severe obesity-inflammatory. Compared with the Healthy phenotype, the Severe dysmetabolic phenotype was independently associated with increased all-cause mortality (HR 1.24, 95% CI 1.05-1.47), whereas the Severe obesity-inflammatory phenotype showed the strongest association with cardiovascular mortality (HR 2.21, 95% CI 1.54-3.17). Kaplan-Meier analyses demonstrated significant differences in survival probabilities across phenotypes (log-rank p < 0.001). Subgroup analyses revealed significant heterogeneity according to age and sex. Competing-risk analyses further supported the association between Severe obesity-inflammatory phenotype and cardiovascular mortality. Distinct metabolic-inflammatory phenotypes demonstrated heterogeneous associations with long-term mortality outcomes. Severe metabolic dysregulation was predominantly associated with all-cause mortality, whereas obesity-related inflammatory burden showed a stronger relationship with cardiovascular mortality.

articles.title: In-hospital management and disposition outcomes for patients with mild traumatic brain injury and isolated traumatic subarachnoid haemorrhage.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: This study aims to review the in-hospital management and disposition of patients with traumatic brain injury (TBI) and a Glasgow coma score (GCS) ≥ 13 with isolated traumatic subarachnoid haemorrhage. Retrospective single-center cohort study, using prospectively collected data from patient charts. All patients admitted to a neurosurgical department at a Danish university hospital, after TBI with radiological confirmed intracranial haemorrhage and GCS ≥ 13, were included. Data on the type of haemorrhage was collected. The outcomes of interest were length of hospital stay (LOS), repeated head CT (RHCT), discharge to in-patient rehabilitation, and neurosurgical intervention. Relative risk (RR) for discharge to inpatient rehabilitation and RHCT was calculated with traumatic subarachnoid haemorrhage (tSAH) as reference for acute subdural haemorrhage (aSDH), traumatic intracerebral haemorrhage (tICH) and epidural haemorrhage (EDH) as a pooled category. In the period April 1st, 2022, to December 31st, 2024, a total of 127 patients were included. The crude RR of discharge to in-patient rehabilitation was 2.6 (95% CI: 1.1-5.8) for the pooled group compared with tSAH. The crude RR of RHCT was 1.3 (95% CI: 1.1-1.6) for the pooled group compared with tSAH. The mean LOS was 2.0 days for tSAH and 3.2 days for the pooled group. Two patients from the pooled group required neurosurgical intervention. In the tSAH group, antiplatelet treatment did not increase the risk of discharge to inpatient rehabilitation. Patients admitted with mild TBI and isolated tSAH have a shorter LOS, lower risk of RHCT, and a lower risk of requiring inpatient rehabilitation at discharge, compared to patients with mild TBI and other types of intracranial haemorrhage. However, the current study is limited to a single-center retrospective design.

articles.title: Expanding minimally invasive options in emergency general surgery: a multicentre evaluation of a novel MIS platform.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: Emergency general surgery (EGS) carries elevated morbidity, and minimally invasive surgery (MIS) may reduce surgical trauma but remains limited by staffing, logistical, and technical barriers. The Maestro® Platform is a collaborative robotic system designed to enhance surgeon autonomy during MIS. This study compares Maestro-assisted versus conventional laparoscopic EGS, stratified by procedure type. This multicentre retrospective study compared 24 Maestro-assisted EGS cases (July 2024-April 2025) with 25 consecutive conventional laparoscopic cases performed by the same surgical team. Outcomes analysed included surgery time, conversion rate, postoperative complications, length of stay, and 30-day mortality. Analysis was stratified by procedure type: appendectomy, emergency colectomy, and small bowel obstruction surgery. Additional Maestro cases without baseline comparators were reported descriptively. Within comparable procedure groups, Maestro-assisted cases showed shorter surgery times: appendectomy (33.5 [31.5-42.3] vs. 76.0 [70.0-81.0] min, p = 0.002), emergency colectomy (135.0 [122.0-165.0] vs. 197.5 [159.3-220.0] min, p = 0.08), and small bowel obstruction (107.0 [28.0-110.0] vs. 108.0 [90.8-127.5] min, p = 0.54). No Maestro cases required conversion to open surgery, compared with 3 of 25 baseline cases (12%). Complication rates and length of stay were similar between groups. No device-related adverse events occurred. In this preliminary procedure-stratified analysis, Maestro-assisted EGS was associated with shorter surgery times and a trend toward shorter length of stay and lower conversion rates in complex procedures such as colectomy, while maintaining comparable safety outcomes. The platform appeared adaptable across diverse emergency indications and may support minimally invasive approaches in emergency settings. Larger, prospective studies will be necessary to confirm these observations and define the role of collaborative robotic platforms in emergency surgical care.

articles.title: Hidden Pitfalls of artificial intelligence in pediatric emergency radiology: a pictorial review of failure modes, clinical implications, and mitigation strategies.
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly transforming diagnostic radiology, yet its current clinical application in pediatric imaging remains fraught with challenges. Considerations that are unique to pediatric patients, including vast variations in developmental anatomy, age-specific disease patterns and pathologies, and technical variability create diagnostic challenges for which many commercially available AI systems, trained predominantly on adult data, are ill-equipped. This review utilizes literature evidence and illustrative clinical cases to critically examine various weaknesses of AI in pediatric imaging. Common pitfalls include misclassification of normal developmental variants, inability to distinguish pathological mimics, vulnerability to motion artifacts, modality-specific limitations, and errors introduced by artifacts or confounders. These failures are amplified by limited pediatric training data, annotation bias, and lack of contextual integration. We propose a structured framework for mitigating these risks, including pediatric-specific data curation, contextual model adaptation, algorithmic transparency, integrated feedback systems, technologist training, case-appropriate sedation planning, and centralized error tracking. These interventions are essential to enable safe, reliable, and ethically responsible AI deployment in pediatric emergency radiology.

articles.title: Non-operative management of penetrating abdominal trauma in a low-volume environment: a single center experience.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: High-volume trauma centers report that selective non-operative management (NOM) in patients suffering from penetrating abdominal trauma (PAT) is a safe approach. Switzerland is a low-volume environment for PAT. We hypothesize that despite the low number of PAT cases, NOM is a feasible approach with comparable outcomes to those in high incidence environments for PAT. Retrospective analysis of patients aged > 16 years who were treated for PAT between January 1, 2013, and December 31, 2023 at a Level I trauma and academic tertiary referral center in a low-volume environment for PAT. The primary endpoint was the failure rate of NOM. Successful NOM was defined as completion of NOM without the need for surgical intervention. Secondary endpoints included the rates of non-therapeutic operations, hospital length of stay and mortality. In total, 57 patients were eligible, with 36 (63.1%) stab wounds (SW), 14 (24.6%) gunshot wounds (GSW) and seven (12.3%) impalements. Median age was 35 years (IQR 24-56) and 73.7% were male. Median ISS was 16 (IQR 4-25). In 28 patients (49.1%) NOM was attempted (23 SW, 1 GSW, 4 impalements). In these patients, median ISS was 4 (IQR 1-16.5), wound localizations were the anterior abdomen in 18 patients (64.3%), the back in 5 patients (17.9%) and the left flank in 4 patients (14.3%). A total of ten patients (35.7%) with NOM were treated as outpatients. In this small cohort there was no instance where this treatment approach had to be changed. In 29 patients (50.9%) primary operative management (POM) was performed (13 SW, 13 GSW, three impalements). Median ISS was 20 (IQR 15-32). There was one non-therapeutic laparotomy and two non-therapeutic laparoscopies. One patient died during surgery due to exsanguination caused by a high-grade liver injury with concomitant lesion of the Vena cava. Selective NOM in patients suffering from PAT appears to be a feasible treatment strategy with favorable outcomes also in a low-volume environment. However, established treatment algorithms, similar to high-volume centers, are required. Possible outpatient care is resource sparing and therefore increasingly important, however, further research is required to investigate its safety and patient selection.

articles.title: Splenic artery embolization versus operative management in traumatic splenic injury: a nationwide trend analysis and hospital-level comparison from Germany, 2019-2025.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: The spleen is the most frequently injured solid abdominal organ in blunt trauma, and its management has evolved substantially over recent decades towards non-operative strategies. Splenic artery embolization (SAE) is recommended by current guidelines as the preferred interventional approach in hemodynamically stable patients with higher-grade splenic injury. Despite this recommendation, national data on SAE utilization in Germany are rare and temporal trends as well as the influence of hospital size on treatment choice have not been systematically described. Nationwide German inpatient data were retrospectively analyzed using the InEK DatenBrowser (datenbrowser.inek.org), covering treatment years 2019 to 2025. All inpatient cases with traumatic splenic injury as the primary diagnosis (ICD-10-GM S36.00-S36.04, S36.08) were identified. Operative management was defined by OPS codes 5-413.* and 5-419.*, SAE by a combination of six OPS codes for selective embolization (particles, coils, and liquid agents). Non-operative management (NOM) comprised all remaining cases. Hospital bed-size categories served as proxies for care level and interventional radiology (IR) infrastructure. A chi-squared test assessed the association between hospital size and SAE utilization. A total of 14,422 inpatient splenic trauma cases were identified between 2019 and 2025 (mean 2,060 per year). SAE cases increased from 50 (4.3% of interventional cases) in 2019 to 81 (6.9%) in 2025, representing a 62% relative increase. Operative case volume remained stable throughout (- 0.9%). Hospital size was a highly significant determinant of SAE utilization (p < 0.001). SAE was effectively absent in hospitals with fewer than 150 beds, reached 2.6-2.7% in regional and secondary care centers, and 14.8% in maximal care and university hospitals. SAE utilization has increased by 62% in Germany between 2019 and 2025, yet remains substantially below guideline recommendations across all hospital categories. The absolute increase in SAE rate corresponded to 1.25% points as a proportion of all splenic trauma cases (95% CI 0.2-2.3 pp). The finding that even major centers with established IR achieved an SAE rate of 14.8% of interventional splenic trauma cases points to persistent structural and process-related barriers. These data support targeted efforts to integrate SAE pathways systematically into certified trauma center care.

articles.title: Utilizing AI Decision Support Tools in Burn Resuscitation: Comparing A Large Language Model to a Computerized Decision Support Tool.
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: Crystalloid resuscitation is central to severe burn care. Traditional approaches rely on calculated formulae, monitoring, and endpoint guided titration. Computerized Clinical Decision Support (CDS) tools automate this process and improve goal-directed outcomes, but use remains limited due to accessibility. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer an unevaluated alternative. This study compared crystalloid estimates between a commonly used LLM and CDS system. A retrospective one-year two phase analysis was conducted for adult patients treated at an ABA-verified burn center who received individualized CDS-guided fluid resuscitation during the first 24 hours after injury. An LLM was queried using standardized prompts based on identical clinical inputs used by the CDS tool, including age, TBSA, weight, formulae, urine output, and confounders. Bland-Altman analysis assessed fluid volume predictions between the LLM and CDS system. This study included eighteen patients with a mean ± SD TBSA burn of 41.7% ± 20.2%, contributing 387 recommendations in Phase 1 and 380 in Phase 2. Mean LLM and CDS system rates through 24 hours post-burn were not statistically significant different (462 ± 318 mL/hr vs 450 ± 288 mL/hr; p=0.57). Correlation between the two systems was strong (r=0.93; 95% CI, 0.91-0.94, p<0.0001) with a mean difference of 12.3 mL/hr (95% limits of agreement, -222 to 246 mL/hr). Following prompt refinement, Phase 2 correlation remained strong (r=0.94; 95% CI, 0.93-0.95, p<0.0001) with a mean difference of -23.4 mL/hr and limits of agreement ranging from -178.3 to 131.5 mL/hr. LLMs can generate sequential fluid-rate recommendations during simulated burn resuscitation, but variability in fluid rates highlight the need for further refinement and clinical validation.

articles.title: Deceased Burn Patients as Organ Donors: Post-Transplant Outcomes.
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: There were 105,459 patients on the transplant waiting list in the United States in 2025. Only 48,149 (~46%) patients received a transplant during 2024. A high demand coupled with a low supply of organs leaves many transplant recipients perpetually on the waiting list. Literature review reveals a small number of studies on organ donation in deceased burn patients. Burn patients with unsurvivable injuries are prone to have multi-system organ failure and sepsis, leading to them often being overlooked for potential organ donation due concern for organ viability. A review of available records from the University of Kansas Medical Center (KUMC), an American Burn Association (ABA) verified center, between 2023 and 2024 yielded 3 deceased burn patients who were evaluated for potential organ donation. A descriptive review of the characteristics of these cases was undertaken. Of the 3 burn patients declared brain dead or switched to Comfort Measure Only (CMO) care and referred for potential organ donation, 3 underwent organ retrieval with 2 having organs subsequently transplanted to recipients. When death is the expected outcome for a burn-injured patient, it is not always top-of-mind for caregivers or family members to consider potential organ donation. Nonetheless, all members of the burn care team should be reminded to consider the possibility of organ donation.

articles.title: Localised geographic and socioeconomic inequalities in prehospital trauma care access for road traffic collisions in England: a spatial autocorrelation analysis.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: We examined national and local associations between socioeconomic deprivation and modelled access to major-trauma resources in England. All 33,755 English Lower-layer Super Output Areas (LSOAs) were analysed. Drive-times to the nearest adult Major Trauma Centre (MTC) and from the nearest listed Helicopter Emergency Medical Service (HEMS) base were computed; flight-time from the nearest HEMS base was estimated. Police-reported killed-or-seriously-injured (KSI) collision rates (2022-2024) and Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD) decile were assessed using global and local spatial autocorrelation. KSI collisions involved at least one killed or seriously injured casualty. Population-based KSI collision rates were spatially clustered (Global Moran's I = 0.207, p = 0.001), while national associations between deprivation and access were weak (bivariate Moran's I = 0.117, 0.023 and - 0.016 for MTC drive-time, HEMS-base road time and flight-time). National median times were 16.4, 20.9 and 4.9 min, respectively. Local analysis identified 1,101 LSOAs (3.4% of 32,747 with valid IMD data) simultaneously more deprived and access-poor across all three measures. Their median own-area times were 56.8, 42.2 and 10.4 min. This subgroup had a higher population-based KSI collision rate than the remainder of the valid-IMD sample (Welch's t = 8.1, p < 0.001), persisting in a rural-only analysis. England showed no national deprivation gradient in access to major-trauma resources. Local analysis identified areas where greater deprivation, slower modelled access and higher KSI collision rates coincided, providing candidates for investigation and service planning.

articles.title: Hidden in plain sight: a comprehensive analysis of missed rib fractures across five anatomic sectors of the chest wall.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: Missed rib fractures on initial chest CT are common and under-reported. We quantified the number, location and severity of rib fractures missed on initial radiologist review compared with a trauma surgeon's systematic secondary review. This retrospective study included patients with rib fractures at three affiliated trauma centers (2023-2024). Trauma surgeons re-reviewed initial chest CT scans using the Sucher-Lim Taxonomy for Acute Rib Fractures (SL-TARF) and compared findings with the original radiologist report. Patients younger than 18 years, with non-acute fractures, not admitted, without CT imaging for review, or without an SL-TARF map recorded by the time of data collection were excluded. Among 943 patients (mean age 63 ± 19 years; 37.4% ground-level falls), 415 (44%) had at least one missed rib fracture. Of 5,588 fractures on secondary review (4,215 reported initially), 1,373 (24.6%) were missed. By sector, missed fractures were costochondral (25.7%), anterior (21.9%), lateral (20.4%), posterior (17.9%) and paravertebral (14.1%). Most were Type 1 (incomplete; 69.1%), then Type 2 (19.2%) and Type 3 (11.7%). Patients with a missed fracture more often had ≥ 7 fractures on the initial report (26.0% vs. 19.1%, p = .011) and flail chest on secondary review (20.0% vs. 6.3%, p < .001). Missed rib fractures occur throughout the rib cage rather than in a single region. Trauma surgeon secondary review of chest CT identifies missed fractures at rates comparable to prior post-mortem or repeat-imaging studies. These findings do not, by themselves, justify a change in practice; larger studies are under way.

articles.title: Failure of intramedullary nailing in pertrochanteric femur fractures - A retrospective analysis of 383 patients over a 5.5-year period.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: Pertrochanteric femoral fractures are a rising health and economic burden in ageing societies. Intramedullary nailing is standard treatment, yet implant failure remains a serious complication. This study evaluated patient, fracture and surgical factors associated with implant failure. This single-centre retrospective cohort study included adults who underwent primary intramedullary nailing for AO/OTA 31A1.2, 31A1.3, 31A2.2 and 31A2.3 pertrochanteric fractures at Evangelisches Krankenhaus Oldenburg, a Level I trauma centre in Oldenburg, Germany, between 1 January 2019 and 31 July 2024. Demographic, clinical and radiographic data were extracted from electronic records and imaging archives. Variables included age, sex, documented osteoporosis, AO/OTA classification, reduction quality and tip-apex distance. Implant failure, including cut-out, migration or loosening was the primary endpoint. Associations were tested using Chi-square and multivariable logistic regression. A total of 383 patients (mean age 80.3 years; 70% women) met inclusion criteria. Osteoporosis was documented in 59%. Implant failure occurred in 4.4% (n = 17), pseudarthrosis in 1.0% (n = 4) and revision surgery in 5.5% (n = 21). In the bivariate Chi-square analysis, fracture morphology was the only parameter significantly associated with implant failure (p < 0.001). In multivariable logistic regression, the model was significant (p = 0.012; Nagelkerke R² = 0.202). Female sex (OR 5.82, p = 0.038) and fracture morphology (p = 0.026) were independent predictors. Fracture morphology described by the AO/OTA classification emerged as the strongest predictor of implant failure after intramedullary nailing of pertrochanteric fractures. Unstable subtypes require careful preoperative planning and follow-up. Female sex was also independently associated with implant failure. Level III, retrospective cohort study (Oxford 2011). German Clinical Trials Register (DRKS), DRKS00024627, retrospectively registered on 29 March 2021.

articles.title: Fragility-associated nonunion represents a distinct biological phenotype compared with trauma-associated nonunion: a retrospective cohort study of 213 consecutive cases.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: Long bone nonunion is conventionally treated as a uniform disease entity. We hypothesized that nonunion arises through distinct biological pathways, with a fragility-associated phenotype driven by systemic biological vulnerability differing fundamentally from a trauma-associated phenotype driven by local soft tissue compromise and infection. Retrospective cohort study of 213 consecutive long bone nonunions treated at a Level 1 trauma center (2007-2018). Patients were classified as fragility-associated (age ≥ 65 years and/or documented osteoporosis; n = 51, 23.9%) or non-fragility/trauma-associated (n = 162, 76.1%). Groups were compared regarding demographics, comorbidity profiles, fracture characteristics, infection rates, operative burden, laboratory parameters, and treatment strategies. Multivariate logistic regression was performed to evaluate independent predictors of septic nonunion and high revision burden. The fragility phenotype was characterized by significantly higher comorbidity burden (3.2 ± 1.6 vs. 1.8 ± 1.6; p < 0.001), cardiovascular disease (90.2% vs. 41.4%; p < 0.001), renal insufficiency (25.5% vs. 3.7%; p < 0.001), elevated CRP (median 11.5 vs. 4.0 mg/L; p = 0.012), and higher ASA classification (ASA ≥ III: 39.2% vs. 19.1%; p = 0.006). The trauma-associated phenotype showed higher rates of open fractures (25.3% vs. 13.7%), polytrauma (27.8% vs. 9.8%; p = 0.014), and nicotine use (47.5% vs. 11.8%; p < 0.001). On multivariate analysis, fragility was not an independent predictor of septic nonunion (OR 1.07, 95% CI 0.44-2.61; p = 0.886) or high revision burden (OR 0.88, 95% CI 0.28-2.75; p = 0.829), while open fracture (OR 3.34, 95% CI 1.40-7.99; p = 0.007) and septic nonunion (OR 25.17, 95% CI 9.14-69.29; p < 0.001) were the dominant risk factors. Fragility-associated and trauma-associated nonunions represent distinct clinical phenotypes. The fragility phenotype is driven by systemic biological vulnerability but does not confer increased infection or reconstructive burden. These findings support phenotype-specific approaches to nonunion prevention and treatment.

articles.title: Characterizing Quality of Life and Psychosocial Burden of Dyschromic Hypertrophic Scarring in Burn Survivors.
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: Dyschromia is a prevalent yet understudied complication of post-burn hypertrophic scarring. Its specific impact on patient-reported outcomes remains uncharacterized, particularly in skin of color. This observational study enrolled 30 adults (≥18 years) with dyschromic hypertrophic scars at a tertiary Burn Center. Participants completed PROMIS questionnaires (Psychosocial Illness Impact, General Life Satisfaction, and Social Isolation), a novel Impact of Dyschromia (IoD) survey, and standardized scar assessments (POSAS, mVSS). Objective scar parameters included total body surface area (TBSA) and melanin index (MI). MI was used to calculate degree of hyper- or hypopigmentation (DOH). Scars were characterized by visibility (high vs. low), and patients were stratified by median IoD scores into low impact (≤55) and high-impact (>55) groups. Participants demonstrated significantly higher psychosocial illness impact (p=0.037) and lower life satisfaction (p=0.041) than normative populations, with significantly worsening scores across 26 of 32 psychosocial illness items pre- vs. post-injury. Scar visibility did not significantly affect psychosocial outcomes (p>0.05). DOH-Hyper correlated negatively with IoD emotional distress and social stigma subdomains (p<0.05), while normal skin MI correlated positively with social stigma (p<0.05). No other objective parameters (TBSA, DOH-Hypo) correlated with IoD scores. The low-impact group had significantly higher DOH-Hyper values (p=0.023), but markedly better PROMIS outcomes across all domains compared to the high-impact group (p<0.05). Dyschromia as a symptom of hypertrophic scarring imposes a significant psychosocial burden on burn survivors. The lack of broad correlation between subjective distress and objective parameters underscores the deeply personal nature of its impact, highlighting the need for systematic psychological screening and individualized care.

articles.title: Recovery and Return to Duty after Mild Frostbite (Cauchy Grades 1-2): A Retrospective Cohort Study in a Military Population.
articles.abstract: BackgroundMild frostbite (Cauchy grades 1-2) is regularly seen in cold exposed military populations, but recovery trajectories and return-to-duty outcomes are poorly described. Understanding the natural course of these injuries is essential to balance operational readiness with personnel safety.MethodsWe conducted a retrospective case series of 54 male service personnel presenting to the UK Defence Cold Injury Clinic with Cauchy grade 1-2 frostbite between March 2023 and June 2025. Data on demographics, injury characteristics, management, recovery during activities of daily living (ADLs), and return to full operational duties, including cold challenge testing outcomes, were extracted and analyzed descriptively.ResultsAmong 46 patients with Cauchy grade 1 frostbite, 33% were symptom-free in ADLs within 1 month, 69% by 2 months, and 89% by 6 months. At 12 months, 98% were symptom-free, with 76% completing cold challenge testing confirming return to full duty. Recovery from Cauchy grade 2 injuries (n = 8) was slower; all remained symptomatic in the first 2 months, 50% were symptom-free by 6 months, and 63% had completed cold challenge testing by 12 months. No patients required surgical intervention, thrombolysis, or iloprost.ConclusionsMild frostbite in military personnel generally resolves within 6 to 12 months, with good functional outcomes. These findings provide evidence to inform structured return to cold pathways for military and other cold-exposed populations.

articles.title: Quantifying Time Saved through Prehospital Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation: A Simulation-Based Analysis in Real-World Cardiac Arrest Patients.
articles.abstract: Extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (eCPR) may improve outcomes in refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) when conventional resuscitation fails. However, in-hospital eCPR is frequently associated with prolonged low flow times due to on-scene assessment, intra-arrest extrication, and transport. Prehospital eCPR aims to reduce these delays, but its potential time advantage remains uncertain. This study evaluates the potential time savings of prehospital eCPR compared with an established in-hospital eCPR program. This prospective observational simulation study was conducted within a high-volume hospital-based eCPR program. Adult OHCA patients meeting pre-defined dispatch criteria were included in a simulated prehospital eCPR cohort and compared with patients undergoing in-hospital eCPR during the same study period. A dedicated eCPR research team was dispatched alongside standard Emergency Medical Services (EMS). For eligible patients, on-scene eCPR decision making and cannulation preparation were simulated, and pre-defined time points were recorded. The primary endpoint was time from emergency call to decision to start sterile field preparation. The secondary endpoint was time to estimated or actual extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) flow, presuming 20 minutes of cannulation duration in the simulation group. Twenty-three patients were included in the simulated prehospital group and 25 in the in-hospital group with comparable baseline characteristics. Time from emergency call to decision was significantly shorter in the simulation group (18 [SD = 5] minutes versus 49 [SD = 9] minutes; P <.001). Time to presumed or actual ECMO flow was also reduced (38 [SD = 5] minutes versus 61 [SD = 9] minutes; P <.001), corresponding to time savings of 31 (95% CI, 26-35) and 23 (95% CI, 18-27) minutes, respectively. In a high-volume metropolitan eCPR system, a prehospital eCPR response has the potential to substantially reduce low flow duration compared with in-hospital pathways. Whether these time savings demonstrated under simulated conditions translate into real-world improved survival and neurological outcomes requires further investigations.

articles.title: From Playgrounds to Projectiles: Epidemiological Pediatric Gunshot Injuries in United States.
articles.abstract: Firearms are the leading cause of death among US children. This study characterizes demographic, psychiatric, and contextual factors associated with pediatric firearm injuries and mortality using the largest trauma cohort to date. Children 18 years or younger with firearm-related injuries were identified in the Trauma Quality Improvement Program (TQIP) database (2017 to 2022). Injuries were categorized by intent, location, and body region using ICD-10 codes. Demographic, mental health, and clinical characteristics were analyzed using the χ2 test. Multivariable logistic regression assessed predictors of in-hospital mortality. Occurrence of firearm injuries over time was also investigated. Among 45,432 injured children, 77.8% were between 15 and 18 years of age; 84.3% were male, and 58.0% were non-Hispanic Black. Medicaid was the most common payer (60.2%). Assault accounted for 70.6% of injuries, followed by unintentional (17.8%) and self-inflicted (4.3%) mechanisms. Overall mortality was 11.8%. The most significant factors associated with mortality on multivariate regression were head injury (OR: 8.78; P<0.001), self-inflicted intent (OR: 6.87; P<0.001), thorax injury (OR: 4.98; P<0.001), and self-pay insurance status (OR: 4.18; P<0.001). Psychiatric comorbidities including mental health diagnoses, ADHD, and alcohol use disorder were each independently associated with decreased odds of mortality (P<0.001). Overall firearm injuries increased over the study period. Non-Hispanic White firearm injuries significantly decreased (19.5% to 13.3%; P<0.001), while non-Hispanic Black injuries simultaneously increased (54.9% to 60.3%; P<0.001). Pediatric firearm injuries represent a multifaceted public health emergency. Injury location and intent are the strongest clinical predictors of mortality, while insurance status and race reflect potential structural disparities. Reducing the burden of pediatric firearm injuries requires coordinated efforts across clinical, legislative, and community domains.

Transition-Phase Injuries and Wilderness EMS Operations During a Mountain Paragliding Festival: A Brief Report.
articles.abstract: IntroductionMountain paragliding festivals concentrate repeated takeoff, flight, and landing activity within terrain-dependent environments, potentially creating complex wilderness emergency medical services (EMS) demands. This brief report characterized festival-associated injury events, flight-phase distribution, environmental conditions, and EMS response requirements during a 2-day international mountain paragliding festival at Mount Babadağ, Turkey.MethodsWe retrospectively reviewed deidentified operational, prehospital, transport, and referral records for all festival-associated paragliding injury events. Variables included patient demographics, flight phase at injury, injury pattern, transport modality, prehospital acuity, and documented EMS resource utilization. Event-period meteorological conditions were summarized using hourly environmental data for the Mount Babadağ coordinate region.ResultsDuring the study period, 4716 paragliding flights and 13 injury events were recorded. The mean patient age was 41.5 ± 6.9 years. Ten injuries (76.9%) occurred during landing, 1 (7.7%) during takeoff, and 2 (15.4%) during sustained flight. Lower-extremity trauma predominated. Three patients were managed onsite, 8 were transported directly by ground ambulance, and 1 underwent maritime-to-ground ambulance transfer. One deceased pilot required helicopter-assisted postmortem recovery. Regional meteorological data showed mild temperatures and relatively low wind speeds.ConclusionsInjuries clustered around terrain-transition phases, especially landing. Mountain paragliding festivals require terrain-aware EMS planning, distributed response capability, and coordinated rescue and recovery resources.

articles.title: Seeing Beyond the Bowel: A Sentinel Loop as a Sonographic Clue to Pancreatobiliary Obstruction.
articles.abstract: The sentinel loop is a localized area of dilated bowel indicating localized abdominal inflammation, traditionally identified on plain films and computed tomography. Despite its diagnostic importance, sentinel loops have not been extensively characterized using point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) in pediatric populations. We report a case of a 3-year-old girl who presented with persistent abdominal pain, initially attributed to constipation. POCUS identified a sentinel loop associated with a choledochal cyst complicated by pancreatobiliary obstruction, an uncommon underlying pathology. Sonographic recognition of the sentinel loop redirected the diagnostic evaluation toward adjacent pathology in this case, illustrating its potential value as a contextual POCUS finding while underscoring the need for cautious interpretation given its nonspecificity and uncertain diagnostic performance.

Comparative validation of five early trauma scores for 24-hour in-hospital mortality in traumatic brain injury.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: Early risk stratification after traumatic brain injury (TBI) is crucial to guide monitoring, escalation of care, and interfacility transfer within the first hours. Bedside scores, including the "Revised Trauma Score (RTS)," "Glasgow Coma Scale, Age, and Systolic Blood Pressure score (GAP)," "modified Rapid Emergency Medicine Score (mREMS)," "Mechanism, Glasgow Coma Scale, Age, and Arterial Pressure score (MGAP)," and "Modified Early Warning Score (MEWS)," are simple and widely available. Prior studies often use mixed trauma cohorts, later endpoints, and provide limited evaluation of calibration or threshold-level clinical utility. TBI-specific head-to-head evidence is therefore needed. The five scores summarize different clinical domains. RTS incorporates the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), systolic blood pressure (SBP), and respiratory rate; GAP incorporates GCS, age, and SBP; mREMS incorporates age, heart rate, respiratory rate, SBP, peripheral oxygen saturation, and GCS; MGAP incorporates injury mechanism, GCS, age, and arterial pressure; and MEWS incorporates routinely measured physiologic and neurologic variables, including blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, temperature, and level of consciousness. Diastolic blood pressure is not a component of any of the five scores evaluated in this study. The component structure and clinical domains of each score are summarized in Supplementary Table S1. This study analyzed consecutive traumatic brain injury admissions in 2024 at a tertiary medical center in Nantong, China (n = 2,287; 24-hour mortality 7.3%). The five bedside scores were recalibrated with a single logistic equation. Performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), the area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC), the Brier score, and calibration intercept and slope, while clinical utility was evaluated as net benefit per 100 patients at 10% and 20% thresholds. All estimates were reported with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) from 1,000 bootstrap resamples, and precision-recall curves were referenced to the cohort prevalence. RTS and GAP showed the strongest discrimination, with mREMS close. RTS 0.874 (95% CI 0.841-0.903), GAP 0.863 (0.831-0.898), mREMS 0.856 (0.826-0.883); MGAP and MEWS were lower (0.632, 0.606). AUPRCs were 0.465 (0.381-0.531) for RTS, 0.382 (0.308-0.453) for GAP, and 0.370 (0.280-0.424) for mREMS (MGAP 0.154 (0.112-0.199); MEWS 0.129 (0.098-0.159)). Brier scores were 0.050, 0.053, and 0.055 for RTS, GAP, and mREMS, respectively. After simple logistic recalibration, calibration intercepts were near 0 and slopes near 1, with observed-vs-predicted curves close to the 45° line across deciles. At 10% and 20% thresholds, RTS and GAP achieved the highest net benefit and more favorable trade-offs per 100 patients; mREMS was intermediate. RTS and GAP showed the best balance of discrimination, calibration, and net benefit at 10% and 20% thresholds; mREMS was comparable after simple recalibration. These findings support prioritizing RTS and GAP for early TBI risk stratification.

articles.title: [When a "minor" injury isn't so minor after all].
Intensive care unit versus ward admission in the elderly patient with one or more rib fractures: Are we too conservative?
articles.abstract: Standardized protocols are often created to triage admission destination of elderly patients with rib fractures. The aim of this study was to assess risk factors for the occurrence of complications and unplanned intensive care unit admission and evaluate adherence to our institution's rib fracture admission algorithm. We hypothesized that adherence to the algorithm was good and that the algorithm correctly identified patients at risk of complications or ward failure. A retrospective study was performed of all patients aged ≥ 65 years admitted with rib fractures between October 1, 2018 and December 31, 2020. Primary outcome was algorithm-adherent triage to the ICU or ward. Subgroup analysis was performed of patients with and without complications. A logistic stepwise regression model was made to identify independent risk factors for adverse in-hospital outcomes. In total, 202 patients were included. A total of 152 patients were correctly triaged following the admission algorithm (75.2%) of whom 124 (61.3%) were triaged to the ICU and 78 (38.6%) were triaged to the ward. 16 of 124 patients (12.9%) were triaged to the ICU in nonadherence with the algorithm, and 31 of 78 patients (39.7%) were triaged to the ward in nonadherence with the algorithm. After logistic regression modeling, age ≥ 77 years, the presence of solid organ injury, and a BPC-18 ≥ 2 were found to improve the algorithm by capturing more complications. After adding these factors, the algorithm captured 94.3% of complications. Adherence to the algorithm was modest at 75%. Over one in four patients developed one or more complications, but the rib fracture-related complication rate was low (3%). Following the algorithm, ward failure rate was low (3%). The addition of specific injury-related variables resulted in capturing > 90% of complications. Further improvement of the algorithm might require a multimodal approach also including frailty-related characteristics.

articles.title: Needlefish Impalement Through the External Auditory Canal: CT Mapping of a High-Risk Penetrating Trajectory.
articles.abstract: Needlefish injuries are uncommon but potentially severe encounters in marine and coastal environments. The fish's elongated, toothed beak can produce a deep penetrating wound with little external evidence of its trajectory, creating an immediate challenge for field stabilization and transport. We describe a 47-year-old fisherman who sustained needlefish impalement through the left external auditory canal. Before referral, the fish body was cut away, while the head and beak were left in situ. Noncontrast computed tomography demonstrated a 7.73 cm calcified beak extending inferomedially through the parotid region to the prevertebral space at C1, with a penetration depth of approximately 5.6 cm and a small cortical defect in the left anterior arch of C1. No intracranial or spinal canal extension, large hematoma, or aerodigestive tract injury was identified. The beak passed close to the carotid vessels, although vascular injury could not be definitively excluded without angiographic imaging. Controlled surgical removal was completed without major vascular or neurologic complication. Complete removal was confirmed. At 1 month, the patient remained clinically well, and magnetic resonance imaging with angiography showed no delayed neurovascular complication. This case supports a practical sequence for marine impalement: stabilize the patient and embedded object, avoid field extraction, shorten only the external portion when necessary for safe transport without disturbing the penetrating segment, and transfer promptly to a center capable of cross-sectional imaging and controlled removal. Computed tomography defines the trajectory, while computed tomography angiography should be considered when major vessels may be involved.

articles.title: Contextualized vs usual cardiopulmonary resuscitation skill stations: a simulation-based, randomized trial.
articles.abstract: We aimed to investigate whether training on a contextualized skill station combined with in-bed cardiopulmonary resuscitation instructions improves the number of excellent chest compressions in a simulated in-hospital cardiac arrest scenario compared to a standard table-based skill station. This randomized, multicenter trial included nurses and nurse assistants from two Danish emergency departments. Participants were trained in chest compressions on a contextualized skill station with the manikin on a bed (intervention) or on a skill station table (control). Participants completed two one-minute sessions with audiovisual feedback, repeated after 2-4 weeks. Skills were assessed in a 2-min in-hospital cardiac arrest scenario 4-8 weeks after the first training session. The primary outcome was the number of excellent chest compressions defined as guideline-compliant depth and rate. We included 65 participants. The intervention group training on the contextualized skill station performed more excellent compressions with a median (quartile 1; quartile 3) of 70 (27; 140) vs 23 (2; 93) (p = 0.01) compared to the control group. In addition, the intervention group performed more compressions with guideline-compliant depth (118 (53; 155) vs 78 (16; 127), p = 0.02), and more compressions with guideline-compliant rate (134 (86; 152) vs 58 (22; 134), p = 0.01) compared to the control group. More participants in the intervention group initiated compressions by jumping onto the bed (85%) compared to the control group (43%), p = 0.002. There was no significant difference in time to first compression. Training on a contextualized skill station with a manikin on a bed significantly increased the number of excellent chest compressions compared to skill station training with the manikin on a table. These findings highlight the importance of integrating clinical factors such as bed adjustments when implementing skill stations for CPR training in emergency departments to facilitate the transfer of skills.

articles.title: Terminology Without Consensus: A Thematic Analysis of Nomenclature Choice and Program Structure Among Expanded EMS Programs in a Single State.
articles.abstract: Expanded emergency medical services (E-EMS) programs, such as mobile integrated health care (MIH) and community paramedicine (CP), are increasingly common in the United States (U.S.). Although an international consensus definition exists specifically for CP, the terminology used by active U.S. E-EMS programs is poorly described, yet has important implications for program visibility, stakeholder engagement, evaluation, and policy. We sought to characterize how E-EMS programs in a single state describe themselves and factors associated with their chosen terminology. We conducted a qualitative thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews with E-EMS programs in Ohio. We used "E-EMS" as a historically established, neutral umbrella term to avoid prespecifying MIH, CP, or MIH-CP terminology during program identification. We identified E-EMS programs through voluntary reports to Ohio EMS, the Emergency Triage, Treat, and Transport (ET3) roster, publicly reported E-EMS programs on national dashboards, and snowball sampling. An interviewee from each E-EMS program participated in a recorded semi-structured interview focused on E-EMS program terminology, goals, services, and partnerships. Interview transcripts were reviewed by two coders, with discrepancies discussed with and adjudicated by a third reviewer. We used an inductive approach to develop the codebook, followed by thematic analysis to identify themes and subthemes. We identified 58 E-EMS programs meeting inclusion criteria; 23 participated and were included in the analysis. Participants described inconsistent use and varying interpretation of common terms such as MIH, CP, or MIH-CP; one in four used alternative terminology (e.g., neighborhood paramedic, EMS outreach). Participants attributed their terminology choices to the variability in MIH definitions and to limited understanding of MIH or CP among patients or external stakeholders. Despite variation in program terminology, program goals were consistently focused on filling unmet community needs, and program services were uniformly described as adaptable and reliant upon partnerships outside of EMS. The terminology used to describe E-EMS programs in a single state varied considerably. Despite this, E-EMS program goals and services were consistent, suggesting early convergence upon the core mission of E-EMS programs. Participants perceived inconsistent or unfamiliar terminology as a barrier to patient awareness, referral generation, and stakeholder engagement.

articles.title: More Than a Tobacco Problem: Cigarette Smoking as a Marker of Poorer Cardiovascular Health Among Emergency Medical Services Clinicians.
articles.abstract: Emergency medical services (EMS) work demands physical capacity, sustained alertness, and performance under stress, making cardiovascular health a workforce concern, not only a personal one. Cigarette smoking persists in portions of the EMS workforce, but whether it signals cardiovascular risk beyond tobacco exposure itself is unknown. We examined whether cigarette smoking was associated with poorer cardiovascular health across the non-tobacco domains of the American Heart Association's Life's Essential 8 (LE8) framework among nationally certified EMS clinicians. We conducted an observational study and cross-sectional secondary analysis of a voluntary survey offered to nationally certified emergency medical technicians (EMTs), advanced EMTs, and paramedics upon completion of recertification (October 2023-April 2024). To isolate associations beyond tobacco exposure, the primary outcome was a modified composite score (mLE7) averaging the seven non-nicotine LE8 domains (0-100 scale). Ideal cardiovascular health was defined as mLE7 ≥ 80. Multivariable linear and logistic regression models adjusted for demographic, educational, occupational, and organizational characteristics. Among 36,436 survey respondents, 7,703 had complete data for smoking status and all seven non-nicotine domains. Of these, 48.8% had never smoked, 45.2% formerly smoked, and 6.0% currently smoked. Mean mLE7 scores were 59.2 among never smokers, 56.9 among former smokers, and 51.5 among current smokers. Compared with never smokers, current smokers had lower adjusted mLE7 scores (β, -6.02; 95% CI, -7.63 to -4.41) and lower odds of ideal cardiovascular health (aOR, 0.37; 95% CI, 0.23 to 0.61). Former smokers had intermediate results (β, -1.62; 95% CI, -2.37 to -0.87; aOR, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.62 to 0.86). Current smoking was associated with poorer scores across diet, physical activity, sleep, blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood glucose domains (p < 0.05). Clinicians at private and hospital-based agencies had lower adjusted mLE7 scores than those at fire-based agencies. Among EMS clinicians, current cigarette smoking was associated with poorer cardiovascular health across nearly every non-tobacco domain, suggesting that smoking may serve as a readily identifiable marker of broader cardiovascular risk in this workforce. Agencies may consider pairing cessation support with broader cardiovascular health initiatives for clinicians who smoke. Sensitivity analyses addressing missing data yielded consistent results.

articles.title: Frequency of On-Scene Goal-Directed Field Interventions for Pediatric Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest in a Regional System of Care.
articles.abstract: Early on-scene resuscitation improves outcomes from pediatric non-traumatic out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA); however, for pediatric patients, the early evacuation strategy remains commonplace. We sought to determine the frequency of goal-directed interventions initiated by paramedics prior to transport for pediatric patients with OHCA in a regional emergency medical services (EMS) system. In this retrospective observational study and cross-sectional analysis, we analyzed the Cardiac Arrest Registry to Enhance Survival (CARES) and linked electronic patient care reports (ePCR) data for patients aged <15 years treated by EMS for nontraumatic OHCA in Los Angeles (LA) County from January 2021 to December 2022. The primary outcome was the frequency of goal-directed therapies administered on scene prior to transport, which we defined as defibrillation for shockable rhythms and administration of epinephrine and fluid resuscitation for non-shockable rhythms. We also tabulated descriptive statistics regarding arrest characteristics, scene times, frequency of other prehospital treatments, and patient outcomes. Among 176 eligible pediatric OHCA cases analyzed in CARES, 112 (64%) were male, the median age was 10 months (IQR 3-51), and 162 (92%) had an initial non-shockable rhythm. Of these, 156 patients were successfully linked to electronic patient care report (ePCR) records for analyses of prehospital interventions. Among 143 patients with non-shockable rhythms, EMS administered epinephrine before transport in 58 (41%) and fluids in 12 (8%). Among 13 patients with shockable rhythms, EMS delivered defibrillation before transport in 11 (85%). Bag-valve-mask (BVM) use was documented in 80 (51%) patients, although its timing relative to scene departure could not be determined. Median on-scene time was 10 minutes (IQR 5-18). Ten patients (6%) survived to hospital discharge, including 6 (3%) with a favorable neurologic outcome. In this regional EMS system, fewer than half of patients with non-shockable rhythms received a dose of epinephrine and fewer than one in ten received intravenous fluids prior to transport, whereas most patients with shockable rhythms were defibrillated on scene. Further work is needed to identify barriers to timely delivery of on-scene resuscitative interventions.

articles.title: Transcutaneous Pacing in the Prehospital Setting: A Retrospective Cohort Study of Electrical Capture.
articles.abstract: Transcutaneous pacing (TCP) treats hemodynamically unstable bradycardia refractory to pharmacologic management. Effective TCP requires electrical and mechanical capture to augment perfusion. Little is known about prehospital TCP and capture incidence. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients treated with prehospital TCP by an emergency medical services agency between 2017 and 2024. Continuous electrocardiogram recordings from cardiac monitors were reviewed. Electrical capture was the primary outcome, defined as a widened QRS with a distinct T wave following a TCP spike. Secondary measures included capture duration, clinician-verbalized pulse during pacing, plethysmograph waveform alignment, and changes in systolic blood pressure (SBP), pulse oximetry, and end-tidal carbon dioxide. Fifty-six patients received attempted TCP. Median age was 70 years (interquartile range [IQR] 58-85), and 34% were female. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) was administered in 59% of patients. Electrical capture was achieved in 18 patients (32%). Among patients who achieved electrical capture, complete capture occurred a mean of 27% (standard deviation 30%) of attempted pacing duration. The median SBP change was +22 (IQR: -2-82) mmHg in patients with electrical capture and 0 (IQR: -29-7) mmHg in those with only rare-to-absent capture (p = 0.031). During TCP, clinicians verbalized a palpable pulse 26 times across 19 patients. Only 4 instances (15%) coincided with electrical capture. Electrical capture during prehospital TCP occurred in a minority of patients and was often intermittent. Prehospital identification of mechanical capture using routine clinical indicators was difficult and unreliable. Future work should standardize capture definitions and physiologic measurements to determine when TCP produces clinically meaningful perfusion.

articles.title: Role of Reticulocyte Hemoglobin to Detect Functional Iron Deficiency in a Parturient with β-thalassemia Trait Undergoing Cesarean Delivery Under Spinal Anaesthesia: A Case Report.
articles.journal: Turkish journal of anaesthesiology and reanimation
articles.abstract: We aimed to report the case of a 29-year-old primiparous woman at 38 weeks' gestation with β-thalassemia trait who was scheduled for elective cesarean delivery under spinal anaesthesia. She had hypochromic microcytic anemia with normal serum ferritin and iron levels, but low transferrin saturation and reticulocyte hemoglobin (Ret-Hb). These findings support iron-restricted erythropoiesis despite normal ferritin levels. Ret-Hb and Ret-Hb factor, considered together with conventional iron indices, helped contextualize the interpretation of anemia, rather than directly determine treatment. This case highlights the perioperative interpretation of discordant iron indices in a pregnant patient with β-thalassemia trait. Multidisciplinary perioperative planning may help avoid unnecessary transfusions or iron supplementation while ensuring preparedness for obstetric blood loss in pregnant patients with thalassemia trait and anemia.

articles.title: Association of electronic versus paper-based documentation with completeness of prehospital emergency physician reports in suspected acute coronary syndrome: a retrospective cohort analysis.
articles.abstract: Complete prehospital documentation supports safe handover, continuity of care, quality assurance, and secondary data use in emergency medical services. This study examined the association between documentation format and record completeness in a physician-staffed prehospital cohort of patients with suspected acute coronary syndrome (ACS), with particular attention to information relevant to hospital handover. We performed a retrospective cohort analysis of 2,787 prehospital emergency physician reports for suspected ACS, recorded in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany, between 1 January 2014 and 31 December 2018. Six records with implausible dates were excluded before primary analysis. The final analytic cohort therefore comprised 2,781 reports: 2,120 from paper-based documentation (PBD) and 661 from electronic-based documentation (EBD). The primary endpoint was complete documentation of a predefined record set comprising hospital destination, prehospital length of stay, initial and handover systolic and diastolic blood pressure, initial and handover peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2), documentation of a 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG), and a numeric pain score (NRS). A sensitivity analysis repeated the endpoint without the NRS. Completeness rates were compared using chi-square tests, and adjusted associations were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression including age, sex, calendar year, and ACS subtype. Overall record completeness was higher in the EBD group than in the PBD group (90.9% vs. 48.2%; p < 0.001), an absolute difference of 42.7% points. The largest between-group differences involved handover blood pressures, handover SpO2, prehospital length of stay, and 12-lead ECG documentation. In the adjusted model, EBD remained associated with higher odds of a complete record (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 10.48, 95% confidence interval [CI] 7.58-14.48; p < 0.001). When the NRS was excluded from the endpoint, completeness remained higher in the EBD group (94.9% vs. 75.6%; aOR 4.40, 95% CI 3.44-5.62; p < 0.001). Electronic documentation was associated with more complete prehospital emergency physician reports in suspected ACS, particularly for handover-relevant variables. However, documentation modality was structurally confounded with treatment site, precluding isolation of an independent technology effect. As this study assessed a process metric rather than clinical outcomes, prospective multicentre studies should determine whether structured electronic documentation improves handover quality, workflow reliability, treatment timeliness, guideline adherence, and patient-centred outcomes. German Clinical Trials Register, DRKS00036944 (MONAH1 study).

articles.title: Out of hospital cardiac arrest following low voltage electrical injury with complete neurological recovery.
articles.abstract: Low voltage electrical injuries are generally associated with minimal or no external burns but may cause severe injury, fatal cardiac arrhythmias and respiratory arrest depending on length of exposure, size of individual, environmental humidity and the cross-sectional area in contact with electrical source. Complete neurological recovery after prolonged resuscitation is uncommon. We report a case of 22 years old male who sustained low voltage electrical injury culminating in out of hospital cardiac arrest. He brought to the emergency department within 10 min after the incident. With initial rhythm of asystole. High quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation started immediately according to advanced cardiac life support guideline; the rhythm converted from asystole to ventricular fibrillation after third cycle of resuscitation requiring three defibrillation attempts. Return of spontaneous circulation was achieved at the end of eighth cycle of resuscitation. Subsequently the patient admitted to intensive care unit and post cardiac arrest care were continued which includes mechanical ventilatory support, hemodynamic support, seizure management, fever prevention. The patient showed progressive neurological improvement and discharged home after three days of stay in intensive care unit with complete neurological recovery. This case shows the critical importance of immediate transport to the hospital, early high-quality CPR and comprehensive post cardiac arrest care for patient survival.

articles.title: Occupational injury history and homelessness among people who beg in Brussels: a cross-sectional study.
articles.abstract: An estimated 400 to 500 people beg on a given day in Brussels, many of whom experience homelessness or housing insecurity. The objective of this study was to estimate the association between a history of occupational injury and homelessness among people who beg in Brussels and have a history of employment. A cross-sectional survey of people who begged in Brussels was conducted in 2021 and 2022 using face-to-face structured interviews. The present analysis was restricted to participants who had ever been employed or reported an occupation. Information was collected on occupational history and work-related health events, current housing status, sociodemographic characteristics, and alcohol and drug problems. Narratives of reported work-related events were reviewed and classified as occupational injuries. A primary definition (Primary) included injuries with clear occupational attribution; an extended definition (Extended) additionally included plausible occupational injuries with less certain attribution. Associations between occupational injury history and homelessness were estimated as prevalence ratios (PR) using Poisson regression with robust standard errors. Models were adjusted for age, gender, age at leaving school, and country of birth. An additional analysis further adjusted for a history of alcohol or drug problems. Participants with missing data for variables included in a given adjusted model were excluded from that analysis. The restricted analysis included 231 participants. Twenty-eight (12%) met the Primary occupational-injury definition and 34 (15%) met the Extended definition. A history of occupational injury was associated with a higher prevalence of homelessness under both definitions. Under the Primary definition, the crude PR was 1.3 (95% CI: 1.0, 1.6) and the adjusted PR was 1.2 (95% CI: 1.0, 1.5; N = 219). Under the Extended definition, the corresponding PRs were 1.3 (95% CI: 1.1, 1.6) and 1.2 (95% CI: 1.0, 1.5). Additional adjustment for a history of alcohol or drug problems yielded PRs of 1.2 (95% CI: 0.9, 1.5) and 1.2 (95% CI: 1.0, 1.5), respectively (N = 213). A history of occupational injury was associated with a higher prevalence of homelessness among people who beg and have a history of employment. Prevention of occupational injuries and better rehabilitation may help avert homelessness.

articles.title: Pediatric Lemierre's syndrome caused by Streptococcus intermedius: a case report.
articles.abstract: Lemierre's syndrome is a rare but life-threatening condition classically caused by Fusobacterium necrophorum. Although members of the Streptococcus anginosus group have been reported as uncommon pathogens, this is, to our knowledge, the first reported pediatric case of Lemierre's syndrome caused by Streptococcus intermedius. This case highlights the diagnostic challenges associated with an atypical microbiologic etiology. A previously healthy 12-year-old male presented to the emergency department with 8 days of fever, headache, and right-sided neck pain following recent travel. On arrival, he was tachycardic and ill-appearing with meningismus, prompting evaluation for meningitis. Computed tomography (CT) of the neck revealed a non-occlusive thrombus of the right internal jugular vein, while a subsequent lumbar puncture was unremarkable. Further evaluation with chest CT demonstrated multiple pulmonary nodules, including a cavitary lesion. Blood cultures grew S. intermedius. The constellation of internal jugular vein thrombosis, septic pulmonary emboli, and bacteremia established the diagnosis of Lemierre's syndrome. The patient was treated with intravenous antibiotics followed by oral therapy without anticoagulation, resulting in clinical and radiographic improvement, normalization of inflammatory markers, and resolution of the internal jugular vein thrombus. This report expands the recognized microbiologic spectrum of pediatric Lemierre's syndrome by identifying S. intermedius as a causative pathogen in what may be the first reported pediatric case. Clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion for Lemierre's syndrome in children presenting with persistent fever and unilateral neck pain, even in the absence of ongoing pharyngitis, as early imaging, blood cultures, and prompt targeted antimicrobial therapy are critical for favorable outcomes.

articles.title: Migration of a Right Ventricular Outflow Tract Stent Causing Incomplete Cardioplegic Arrest: Stent Gone Astray!
articles.journal: Turkish journal of anaesthesiology and reanimation
articles.abstract: Right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) stenting is an established palliative option in tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) when surgical repair poses a high-risk. We report a rare, life-threatening complication in a 4-year-old child with TOF, a hypoplastic pulmonary annulus, and multiple comorbidities that precluded primary corrective surgery. RVOT stenting was therefore planned. During catheterization, the stent embolized, necessitating emergency surgical retrieval. Intraoperatively, the stent was seen lodged across the aortic valve, preventing complete leaflet coaptation, and causing the cardioplegia to leak into the left ventricle. This resulted in an incomplete cardioplegic arrest. Real-time transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) identified the mechanism of cardioplegia failure, delineated the stent position, guided its repositioning, and facilitated successful cardioplegia delivery and definitive surgical repair. This case emphasizes meticulous anatomical evaluation and highlights the indispensable role of intraoperative TEE in high-risk RVOT stenting.

articles.title: Needed: New Guidelines for Greater Health Security in a Climate-Changed World.
articles.abstract: Climate change is already giving dramatic proof of the myriad of severe threats it poses to health and health security. Effective institutional guidelines are essential to help hospitals, public health departments, and other health service organizations build the capacity and resilience needed to protect the American population from those dangers. Review of 30 evaluation studies shows, however, that 16 pertinent existing sets of guidelines have had uncertain success in addressing health threats that predate the climate change era. US health leaders and policymakers should take corrective actions to: (1) create a standing research program dedicated to developing guidelines and related incentives that can help strengthen health sector climate resilience and progressively improve health outcomes; (2) revamp the current Medicare and Medicaid conditions of participation to ensure that hospitals, public health departments, and other health providers adapt effectively to climate change; and (3) require that health guideline organizations and health service providers that receive public funding publish annual reports on their progress toward meeting those goals.

articles.title: Daytime Sleepiness and Self-Reported Sleep Characteristics Among Emergency Healthcare Workers in Public and Private Hospitals in Sana'a, Yemen.
articles.abstract: To describe daytime sleepiness and self-reported sleep characteristics among emergency healthcare workers in Sana'a, Yemen, and examine unadjusted differences between public- and private-hospital participants. This cross-sectional study included 198 physicians, nurses, and respiratory therapists selected by convenience sampling from six hospitals during February-June 2026. Responses to the eight-item Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) were summed only when all items were valid. Sleep latency, duration, and perceived sleep quality were analyzed as recorded categorical responses. Standard Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) global scores were not reconstructed because required continuous timing responses were not available. Comparisons used Welch's t test and Mann-Whitney U-tests. Complete valid ESS totals were available for 193 participants (mean 8.98 ± 4.13); 77/193 (39.9%) scored >10. Among respondents with valid item data, 143/197 (72.6%) reported <6 hours of sleep, 85/197 (43.1%) reported sleep latency >30 minutes, and 44/194 (22.7%) rated their sleep as fairly or very bad. Mean ESS scores were 9.25 ± 3.87 (public, n=101) and 8.68 ± 4.41 (private, n=92); difference 0.56 points (95% CI -0.62 to 1.75; Welch p=0.349). Hospital sector was strongly confounded with profession, shift pattern, and working hours in the available dataset. Short reported sleep duration, prolonged sleep latency, and ESS-defined excessive daytime sleepiness were common in this convenience sample. Neither comparable global PSQI results nor independent sector effects could be established. Further studies should retain standard validated questionnaire responses and strengthen the sampling design.
